title: How To Be More Charismatic
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explores why some teachers seem naturally charismatic and argues the difference is not innate talent but a single behavior: embracing one's authentic self in the classroom. He notes that fear, nerves, or the belief that effective teaching requires a buttoned-up persona causes many teachers to strip away their real personality the moment they stand in front of students, which makes them uninteresting and hard to connect with. While staying within professional bounds, he urges teachers to let more of their genuine quirks, vulnerabilities, and idiosyncrasies show through, arguing these perceived weaknesses are actually a teacher's greatest strengths. He preempts the excuse that some people simply aren't natural teachers, describing himself as introverted, awkward, and unpolished, yet effective because of—not despite—those traits. The piece frames charisma as the inward acceptance and outward expression of one's true self, requiring only courage rather than any special gift.
points: Charisma is reframed not as an innate trait but as the willingness to let one's authentic personality show through in the classroom.
Many teachers strip away their real personality out of fear or the belief that good teaching requires a buttoned-up persona, making them uninteresting to students.
A teacher's quirks, vulnerabilities, and perceived weaknesses are described as their greatest strengths for building charisma.
Linsin counters the common excuse that charisma requires natural talent by describing himself as introverted, awkward, and unpolished, yet effective.
Becoming more charismatic requires only courage and a refusal to be anything but authentically oneself, not any special skill.
quotes: There are teachers who seem blessed with natural charisma. The lucky ones.
Whatever the reason, they become almost entirely stripped of their true personality.
This is a big problem. Because when you inhabit a teaching persona that is different from your natural self, you become uninteresting and hard for students to pay attention to.

The truth is, you are charismatic. Just as you are . In fact, it’s your uniqueness, your quirks and idiosyncrasies, your vulnerability and eccentricity, even your perceived weaknesses that are your greatest strengths.
I’m nothing special. I’m introverted by nature. I’m not a smooth talker. I’m frequently awkward. Again, doesn’t matter. In fact, these very things help endear me to my students.
Charisma is nothing more than the inward acceptance and outward expression of the best of who you really are.
